title: Requirements after sign-off: quality, traceability and checking that it worked
summary: Sign-off is a checkpoint. How to write requirements people can test, prioritize honestly, trace them through change, and check that the shipped solution worked.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The sign-off email lands at 5:42 p.m. Requirements approved, next phase ready, half the department in CC. Two weeks later the team finds out that "export customer data" meant a CSV file to one stakeholder, an Excel report to another, an API feed to engineering and a redacted extract to compliance.

Nobody lied and nobody was careless. The sentence was just loose enough for four people to read four different things into it. That's the half of business analysis that gets the least attention: after the document is approved, the requirement still has to survive quality checks, prioritization, change, testing, rollout, and a hard look at whether the business outcome ever showed up.

Source note: This series comes from my study notes on Lean Business Analysis, which pull together ideas from Emrah Yayici, PMI and Business Analysis For Dummies. Where a point comes from a public standard or a practitioner's article, I link it directly. Treat these posts as working notes and go to the books for the full picture.

A requirement can sound complete and still be vague

Start by knowing which level a requirement lives at. IIBA's requirements infographic, which summarizes section 2.3 of the BABOK Guide v3 (Requirements Classification Schema), uses four categories (IIBA, Requirements infographic):

  • Business requirements: goals, objectives and outcomes that explain why the change exists.
  • Stakeholder requirements: what particular groups need so the business requirements can be met.
  • Solution requirements: the capabilities (functional) and qualities (non-functional) the solution must have.
  • Transition requirements: what it takes to move from the current state to the future state, such as data conversion and training. They're temporary and drop away once the change is done.

Mixing levels causes a lot of confusion. "Improve renewal retention" and "email a reminder seven days before the contract expires" can both be valid. They answer different questions, and the second one only earns its place if it serves the first.

Then check quality. A useful requirement is clear, consistent with the rest, correct, complete enough for its purpose, feasible, testable and actually needed. Karl Wiegers, in his article "10 Requirements Traps to Avoid", names the usual suspects: words like "minimize, maximize, optimize, rapid, user-friendly, easy, simple" feel precise to whoever writes them and give a tester nothing to check. His fix is to have a team with different perspectives formally inspect the requirements documents (Wiegers, 10 Requirements Traps to Avoid, trap 3). You don't need legal language. You need sentences the team can build, test and accept without guessing.

Weak requirementProblemStronger version
The system shall be fast.Nothing to measureThe search results page returns the first 50 matching records within two seconds for 95 percent of requests under normal load.
Users can export data.Four people, four readingsAccount managers can export filtered customer renewal records to CSV, with the columns currently visible in the table.
High-risk customers need approval.The rule is never definedCustomers with overdue invoices above 10,000 dollars, or with an active legal hold, need finance approval before a renewal discount applies.

Prioritization protects focus

If nobody is watching, prioritization turns into a contest that the loudest stakeholder wins. Simple tools help: MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't for now), multivoting to narrow a long list, or weighted scoring when the criteria are written down first.

The trap is labels with no consequences. Wiegers quotes a user representative who says "They're all important, or I wouldn't have given them to you," and lists as a warning sign that more than 90% of your requirements are classified as high priority (same article, trap 4). If everything is a Must, nothing is. A stricter test for Must: without this, is the release legally invalid, commercially pointless, unusable in daily operations, or unsafe? If the answer is no on all four, it can still matter a lot. It just isn't a Must.

Say you're planning the first release of an internal procurement tool. "Create a purchase request", "approve a request" and "audit approval history" are probably Musts. "Dashboard by department", "bulk vendor import" and "custom email templates" can be Should or Could, depending on what the rollout needs. A small, clear first release usually serves people better than a heroic one.

Traceability keeps the promise connected

Traceability is the thread from a business need to a requirement, then to design, build items, test cases, the release and the outcome. Done mechanically, it feels like paperwork. It pays off the day something changes. The same IIBA summary, citing BABOK section 5.1 (Trace Requirements), gives two reasons to bother: tracing makes impact analysis easier when something changes, and it helps you prioritize design and development. Wiegers says it more bluntly: make sure you can trace every functional requirement back to its origin (trap 5).

A traceability matrix can hold the requirement ID, source, business objective, priority, owner, status, linked design, linked tests, release and change history. In a small product team that might be Jira links plus a short table. In a regulated environment you'll need stricter baselines and approvals.

The value shows up in questions like these:

  • If we drop this requirement, which business objective takes the hit?
  • If this regulation changes, which screens, rules, data fields and tests have to change with it?
  • If this test fails, which stakeholder promise is now at risk?
  • When someone asks for a "new" feature, is it new scope or a fix to a need we already approved?

Traceability also keeps scope creep in check, because it shows the impact of a change before anyone says yes. A change request should be weighed against value, effort, risk, timeline, downstream dependencies, test coverage, training and operational readiness.

Change control is how change stays honest

Lean BA adapts, and adapting still needs some discipline. Once requirements are baselined, a change needs a path. Wiegers suggests a change control board that reviews proposed changes at regular intervals, plus the habit of analyzing the impact of each proposed change before anyone commits to it (traps 8 and 9). In a small team the "board" might be a product trio or two delivery leads. What matters is that decisions are deliberate and visible.

A short impact analysis asks:

  1. What exactly is changing?
  2. Which requirement, rule, process, data, interface or stakeholder does it touch?
  3. What happens if we accept it now, defer it, or reject it?
  4. Which tests, training, reports, integrations or operating procedures have to change?
  5. Who has the authority to decide?

You're protecting the team from promises made in a hallway and never written down. Wiegers calls those "requirement changes that sneak in through the back door", and warns that if sign-off on the requirements is "just a game or a meaningless ritual", you can expect a continuous wave of changes (trap 7).

Solution evaluation starts before go-live

Solution evaluation asks whether what you delivered actually meets the need. That question shouldn't wait for launch. Acceptance criteria, test scenarios, prototypes, walkthroughs, exploratory testing and UAT all give you earlier signals.

Teams often treat UAT as the users' final blessing. It's more useful as a check that the solution supports real business use. Day-in-the-life testing goes one step further: you walk through an ordinary workday with real roles and realistic data, including the interruptions, handoffs, corrections, reports and recovery paths that never make it into a happy-path script.

After release, compare expected with actual. Did cycle time drop? Did the error rate fall? Are people working around the system with their old spreadsheets? Did support tickets just move from one queue to another? Did the new process push a problem somewhere else?

Transition is part of the solution

A solution nobody can adopt isn't finished. Transition requirements, the temporary category from the BABOK schema above, cover data migration, training, support, communication, cutover, rollback, operational handover and retiring the old process or system.

Your rollout strategy shapes how much can go wrong at once:

  • Parallel run: old and new run side by side for a while. Safest, and the most expensive.
  • Pilot: a small group goes first, so problems hit fewer people and feedback arrives early.
  • Single cutover: fastest, and the riskiest.
  • Hypercare: a short window of focused support right after go-live, when real use shows what planning missed.

The earlier posts in this series set up what you're tracing here: planning, stakeholders and elicitation covers where requirements come from, and requirements modeling covers the diagrams that make them easier to check. For this week, pick one approved requirement in your current project and follow it forward to a test case and back to a business goal. If either link is missing, you've found your first traceability gap, and it's much cheaper to fix now than after go-live.

faqs.q: What makes a requirement high quality?
faqs.a: It's clear, consistent with other requirements, correct, complete enough for its purpose, feasible, testable and actually needed. In practice, avoid subjective words like "fast", "easy" or "user-friendly" and replace them with something a tester can check, such as a response time for a stated share of requests.

Traceability links a business need to its requirements, designs, build items, tests, releases and outcomes. IIBA's summary of BABOK v3 section 5.1 gives two main benefits: easier impact analysis when something changes, and help prioritizing design and development.

faqs.q: Why does change control matter for requirements?
faqs.a: It makes each change a deliberate decision. Before committing, the team looks at what changes, what it touches, what happens if it's accepted, deferred or rejected, what tests and training must change, and who has the authority to decide. Karl Wiegers recommends a change control board and an impact analysis for every proposed change.

faqs.q: What is solution evaluation in business analysis?
faqs.a: It checks whether a proposed or delivered solution meets the business need. It starts before go-live with acceptance criteria, UAT and day-in-the-life testing, and continues after release by comparing expected and actual results such as cycle time, error rate and workarounds.
